title: The verb “to be”
explanation: Use “to be” to describe people and things. I take am; he/she/it takes is; we/you/they take are. Make it negative with not and questions by putting be first.
tip: Contractions are natural: I'm, he's, we're, isn't, aren't.

title: Present simple
explanation: Use the present simple for habits, routines and facts. Add -s for he/she/it. Use do/does to form questions and negatives.
tip: Only the he/she/it form takes -s: he runs, but they run.

title: Articles: a, an, the
pattern: a/an + singular noun (first mention) · the + known noun
explanation: Use a before a consonant sound and an before a vowel sound for one non-specific thing. Use the when it's clear which one you mean.
tip: It's about sound, not spelling: an hour, a university.

practice.q: Close ___ door, please. (we both know which)

title: Plurals & there is / there are
pattern: there is + singular · there are + plural
explanation: Most nouns add -s for plural (some add -es or change form). Use there is for one thing and there are for more than one.
examples: There is a book on the table.
tip: Irregular plurals don't take -s: child→children, man→men, foot→feet.

practice.q: There ___ two cats in the garden.

title: Present continuous
explanation: Use the present continuous for actions happening now or around now. Form it with be + the -ing form of the verb.
tip: Compare with present simple: “I read every day” (habit) vs “I'm reading now” (now).

title: Past simple
explanation: Use the past simple for finished actions at a known past time. Regular verbs add -ed; many common verbs are irregular. Use did for questions and negatives.
examples: She went to Paris last year.
tip: After did, always use the base verb: “Did you go?” not “Did you went?”

title: Comparatives & superlatives
pattern: short adj + -er than · the + adj + -est · more/most + long adj
explanation: Compare two things with the comparative (-er / more) and three or more with the superlative (the -est / the most).
examples: This box is heavier than that one.
She is more careful than me.
That was the most interesting talk.
tip: One syllable → -er/-est; three+ syllables → more/most. Good→better→best is irregular.

practice.q: It's the ___ film I've ever seen.

title: Future: will vs. be going to
pattern: will + base verb · am/is/are going to + base verb
explanation: Use will for decisions made now, offers and predictions. Use be going to for plans already decided and predictions based on evidence.
examples: We're going to visit Rome in May.
Look at those clouds — it's going to rain.
tip: Plan already made → going to. Deciding as you speak → will.

practice.q: We ___ buy a house next year (already decided).

title: Present perfect
explanation: Use the present perfect for past actions connected to now: life experience, recent news, or unfinished time. Use for + a period and since + a starting point.
tip: Use the past simple for a finished time (“I saw it yesterday”), present perfect for unfinished/unstated time (“I have seen it”).

title: Modal verbs (can, must, should)
explanation: Modals add meaning to a verb: can/could (ability, possibility), must/have to (obligation), should (advice), might/may (possibility). They are followed by the base verb with no -s.
tip: No “to” and no -s after a modal: “She can swim,” not “She cans to swim.”

title: Zero & first conditional
pattern: If + present, present (zero) · If + present, will + base (first)
explanation: Use the zero conditional for facts that are always true. Use the first conditional for a real or likely future situation and its result.
examples: If you heat ice, it melts.
If it rains, the ground gets wet.
If you study, you will pass.
I'll call you if I have time.
tip: No “will” in the if-part: “If it rains, I will stay,” not “If it will rain…”.

practice.q: If you mix blue and yellow, you ___ green.

title: Second conditional
pattern: If + past simple, would + base verb
explanation: Use the second conditional for unreal, imaginary or unlikely present/future situations. The past form here means “imaginary”, not past time.
examples: If I had more money, I would travel.
If I were you, I'd apologise.
She would help if she knew.
What would you do if you won?
tip: With “to be”, formal English uses were for all subjects: “If I were rich…”.

practice.q: If I ___ you, I'd take the job.
If we had a car, we ___ drive there.

title: Third conditional
pattern: If + past perfect, would have + past participle
explanation: Use the third conditional to imagine a different past — something that did NOT happen and its imagined result. It often expresses regret or criticism.
examples: If I had studied, I would have passed.
She would have come if you had invited her.
If they hadn't left early, they'd have missed the train.
tip: Both parts are unreal past: “had + p.p.” in the if-part, “would have + p.p.” in the result.

practice.q: If he ___ harder, he would have won.

title: The passive voice
pattern: subject + be (correct tense) + past participle (+ by …)
explanation: Use the passive when the action matters more than who does it, or the doer is unknown/obvious. The object of the active sentence becomes the subject.
examples: The results will be announced tomorrow.
tip: Keep the tense in “be”: is made, was made, has been made, will be made.

practice.q: This song ___ by millions of people.

title: Reported speech
pattern: say/tell + that + clause (tense usually shifts back)
explanation: When we report what someone said, the tense usually moves one step back (present→past, will→would) and pronouns/time words change.
examples: “I am tired.” → He said he was tired.
“I'll call.” → She said she would call.
“We saw it.” → They said they had seen it.
tip: Tell needs a person (tell me), say does not (say that…).

practice.q: “I like it.” → He said he ___ it.
“I will help.” → She said she ___ help.

title: Relative clauses
explanation: Relative clauses add information about a noun. Use who for people, which for things, that for either (in defining clauses), where for places and whose for possession.
examples: The man who called is my boss.
The book which I read was great.
This is the house where I grew up.
She's the writer whose book won.
tip: In a defining clause you can drop who/which/that when it's the object: “the book (that) I read”.
